The Book of Job is a biblical wisdom text exploring the problem of human suffering and divine justice. It tells the story of Job, a righteous man afflicted with undeserved calamity. Job endures devastating losses: his wealth, health, and family, yet refuses to curse God despite the advice of his friends. Job's three friends—Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar—visit to console him but instead argue that his suffering must result from sin, pushing the conventional wisdom of retributive justice. Job vehemently protests his innocence, demanding that God explain why a just God would permit undeserved suffering to befall a faithful servant. A mysterious character named Elihu appears to offer a fourth perspective, suggesting suffering serves purposes of divine discipline and instruction beyond human comprehension. God finally speaks from a whirlwind, overwhelmingly cataloging the wonders of creation and asking Job whether he can comprehend divine wisdom and cosmic order. The book ends with Job's vindication, humility, and restoration, though it never provides a complete intellectual answer to the problem of evil that inspired the inquiry. Instead, it emphasizes the limits of human understanding when confronted with divine sovereignty.
